articles.title: Global Ship Lease secures newbuilding finance
articles.summary: Global Ship Lease has agreed a US$1 billion syndicated loan facility to finance 15 containership newbuildings scheduled for delivery between late 2028 and 2030. The seven-year facility carries an interest rate of SOFR plus 1.5%. Global Ship Lease intends to draw the financing in tranches as each vessel is delivered....
articles.body: Global Ship Lease has agreed a US$1 billion syndicated loan facility to finance 15 containership newbuildings scheduled for delivery between late 2028 and 2030. The seven-year facility carries an interest rate of SOFR plus 1.5%. Global Ship Lease intends to draw the financing in tranches as each vessel is delivered. All 15 ships have secured time-charter employment commencing shortly after delivery. Eight banks support Global Ship Lease loan The oversubscribed facility is backed by an eight-bank syndicate. Bank of America serves as bookrunner, mandated lead arranger, facility agent and security agent. Bank of China (Hong Kong), KfW IPEX and ABN AMRO also act as mandated lead arrangers. CTBC and CaixaBank serve as lead arrangers, while BOCOM Hong Kong and First Citizens Bank participate as arrangers. Tassos Psaropoulos, Chief Financial Officer of Global Ship Lease, said the financing further reduces the risk associated with the company’s newbuilding programme while providing competitive terms and diversified lender support. “The oversubscribed facility involves top-tier banks spanning three continents,” said Psaropoulos. He added that matching each loan tranche with vessel delivery and the commencement of its charter provides greater certainty from both cash-flow and risk-management perspectives. According to the company, the facility’s lending margin is 550 basis points lower than the financing terms available to Global Ship Lease five years ago.
takeaways: Global Ship Lease has agreed a US$1 billion syndicated loan facility to finance 15 containership newbuildings scheduled for delivery between late 2028 and 2030.
The seven-year facility carries an interest rate of SOFR plus 1.5%.
Global Ship Lease intends to draw the financing in tranches as each vessel is delivered.

articles.title: Matson christens new Aloha Class containership Makua
articles.summary: Matson and Hanwha Philly Shipyard have christened Makua, the first of three new Aloha Class containerships being built for the carrier’s Hawaii and China–Long Beach Express services. Matson board member Jenai Wall officially christened the vessel during a ceremony at the Philadelphia shipyard on 10 October. Around...
articles.body: Matson and Hanwha Philly Shipyard have christened Makua , the first of three new Aloha Class containerships being built for the carrier’s Hawaii and China–Long Beach Express services. Matson board member Jenai Wall officially christened the vessel during a ceremony at the Philadelphia shipyard on 10 October. Around 300 guests attended the event, including government representatives, company executives, shipyard employees and union leaders. Matson advances fleet renewal programme The three Jones Act-compliant vessels represent an investment of approximately US$1 billion. They will replace three ships currently operating across Matson’s Hawaii and China–Long Beach Express networks. Makua is scheduled for delivery during the first quarter of 2027. The second vessel is expected in the third quarter of 2027, followed by the third ship in the second quarter of 2028. The other two vessels will be named Malama and Makena . “We look forward to putting Makua to work serving our customers early next year,” said Matt Cox, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Matson. He added that the three vessels would improve operating efficiency, reliability and capacity across the carrier’s core services. Aloha Class specifications The new Aloha Class ships will offer a capacity of 3,600 TEUs and measure approximately 259 metres in length. With a top speed approaching 24 knots, they will rank among Matson’s fastest vessels. Each ship will feature dual-fuel engines capable of operating on conventional marine fuel or LNG. Additional environmental features include a fuel-efficient hull design, double-hull fuel tanks and freshwater ballast systems. Unlike Matson’s two existing Aloha Class vessels, which required modifications for LNG operation, the three new ships will be delivered LNG-ready.
takeaways: Matson and Hanwha Philly Shipyard have christened Makua , the first of three new Aloha Class containerships being built for the carrier’s Hawaii and China–Long Beach Express services.

articles.body: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd will relaunch the FM1 service under the Gemini Cooperation, restoring direct connectivity between Asia and the Middle East. The relaunched service will connect major Asian gateways with Khor Fakkan in the United Arab Emirates. The rotation will be: Qingdao – Ningbo – Tanjung Pelepas – Khor Fakkan – Singapore – Qingdao First FM1 sailing The first sailing will be operated by Maersk Athabasca on voyage 642W. The vessel is scheduled to depart Qingdao on 17 October 2026 and arrive at Khor Fakkan on 16 November. The FM1 relaunch will provide additional direct ocean capacity to Khor Fakkan. Maersk’s existing inland transportation services will provide onward connections to destinations across the Upper Gulf. Existing booking restrictions and cargo acceptance guidelines for the Middle East will remain in effect. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said they would continue monitoring the regional security situation. Further adjustments to Gemini Cooperation services will remain subject to developments across the Middle East.
takeaways: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd will relaunch the FM1 service under the Gemini Cooperation, restoring direct connectivity between Asia and the Middle East.

articles.title: Rosatom takes full control of Delo Group in major Russian logistics consolidation
articles.summary: Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom has acquired full ownership of Delo Group, one of the country’s largest container transport and logistics operators, as it moves to consolidate its shipping, port and rail assets under a broader logistics structure. The transaction, announced on 7 October 2026,...
articles.body: Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom has acquired full ownership of Delo Group, one of the country’s largest container transport and logistics operators, as it moves to consolidate its shipping, port and rail assets under a broader logistics structure. The transaction, announced on 7 October 2026, involved Rosatom acquiring the remaining 51% stake in Delo Group from its founder, Sergei Shishkarev. Rosatom previously held a 49% interest in the company. The acquisition gives Rosatom complete control of a logistics group with extensive container terminal operations, inland transport infrastructure and a substantial fleet of containers and railway platforms. Rosatom plans to consolidate Delo and FESCO assets Following the transaction, Rosatom intends to bring Delo Group together with its existing logistics businesses, including shipping and transport operator FESCO. Rosatom Director General Alexei Likhachev confirmed the completion of the acquisition and said the corporation was beginning the final consolidation of its logistics assets, with the objective of establishing Russia’s largest national logistics company. According to Likhachev, the corporation’s logistics operations now account for approximately 50% of Russia’s container handling market and 44% of the country’s rail container transport market. These figures represent the company’s own assessment of its market position. The proposed consolidation would bring together Delo’s container terminal and rail operations with FESCO’s maritime services, port infrastructure and intermodal transport network. Rosatom also has responsibility for developing the Northern Sea Route, making maritime and inland logistics an increasingly important part of its wider activities. articles.body: Hutchison Ports and MSC’s terminal investment arm, Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), have resumed discussions over the proposed Omega container terminal project in Rotterdam, reviving negotiations over a major expansion of container handling capacity at Europe’s largest port. The development was disclosed by Dutch trade unions FNV Havens and CNV following a meeting with Hutchison Ports Delta II management on 1 October 2026. Although discussions have restarted, the companies have not announced a final agreement or investment decision, leaving the project’s future uncertain. Rotterdam seeks clarity on Omega project According to FNV Havens, Hutchison Ports Delta II management confirmed that negotiations with TiL had resumed but did not provide details about their content or progress. The union also reported that, according to management, the Port of Rotterdam Authority wants clarity on whether the project will proceed before 1 January 2027. During the meeting, management indicated that the port authority could offer the site to other interested parties if the project does not move forward. However, FNV expressed doubts about the reliability of the proposed deadline, noting that previous timelines for a decision had been extended. The renewed negotiations follow a prolonged period of uncertainty over the project’s development and the future of employees at Hutchison Ports Delta II. Proposed terminal could handle up to 7 million TEU The Omega project was originally announced in August 2022 as a joint development between Hutchison Ports and TiL, the terminal investment subsidiary of Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC). articles.title: CMA CGM announces rate increases on Oceania–Americas trades
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced new Rate Restoration Initiatives (RRI) of US$300 per TEU on container shipments between Oceania and the Americas, effective 2 November 2026. The rate adjustments cover cargo moving in both directions, including shipments from Oceania to North and Latin America and shipments from the eastern...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Rate Restoration Initiatives (RRI) of US$300 per TEU on container shipments between Oceania and the Americas, effective 2 November 2026. The rate adjustments cover cargo moving in both directions, including shipments from Oceania to North and Latin America and shipments from the eastern coasts of the United States and Canada, as well as the US Gulf, to Oceania. According to the French shipping company, the adjustments will apply to tariff and service contract rates within the scope of the respective announcements. Rate increases on both trade directions For shipments originating in Oceania, CMA CGM will implement an RRI of US$300 per TEU on cargo destined for the US East Coast, Canada East Coast, US Gulf and Latin America. The same increase will apply to shipments moving in the opposite direction, from the US East Coast, US Gulf and Canada East Coast to Oceania. Both initiatives will take effect on 2 November 2026. The adjustments cover dry containers, refrigerated cargo, out-of-gauge (OOG) shipments and paying empty containers. The carrier has not specified individual ports or an expiry date for either initiative. The announced measures will affect applicable freight rates on the designated routes, with the same US$300 per TEU adjustment applying in both directions.
takeaways: CMA CGM has announced new Rate Restoration Initiatives (RRI) of US$300 per TEU on container shipments between Oceania and the Americas, effective 2 November 2026.
According to the French shipping company, the adjustments will apply to tariff and service contract rates within the scope of the respective announcements.

articles.title: Hapag-Lloyd details revised ZIM proposal to address Israeli concerns
articles.summary: Hapag-Lloyd CEO Rolf Habben Jansen has outlined further details of the company’s revised proposal to acquire Israeli container shipping company ZIM, including plans to strengthen Israel’s maritime capabilities and address concerns raised by government authorities. The revised proposal, developed jointly with Israeli...
articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd CEO Rolf Habben Jansen has outlined further details of the company’s revised proposal to acquire Israeli container shipping company ZIM, including plans to strengthen Israel’s maritime capabilities and address concerns raised by government authorities. The revised proposal, developed jointly with Israeli investment firm FIMI, includes an additional shipping route to Asia, investment in Israeli maritime personnel and a new fleet for ZIM Israel. Habben Jansen said the changes were designed to address Israel’s national security requirements and provide greater maritime independence. “The substantially improved proposal gives Israel materially more maritime independence and addresses all its national security needs,” he said. The Hapag-Lloyd CEO also emphasized the importance of retaining shipping expertise in Israel as part of the proposed transaction. Revised proposal to be presented to Israeli authorities Habben Jansen addressed concerns raised by Israel’s Ministry of Finance and Government Companies Authority (GCA), arguing that their positions were based on the original acquisition proposal. According to the executive, the revised structure incorporates significant changes made in response to those concerns. All details of the improved proposal are still being developed and will be submitted and explained to the relevant Israeli authorities over the coming weeks. “We are confident that the strengthened proposal addresses the concerns raised and will pave the way for approval of the transaction,” Habben Jansen said. However, the transaction remains subject to the necessary approvals, and the revised proposal has not yet received final clearance. articles.title: South Korea completes Arctic container voyage as commercial challenges emerge
articles.summary: South Korea has completed its first container shipping round trip between Asia and Europe via the Northern Sea Route, with the PanStar Acro returning to Busan after a 50-day voyage that highlighted both the operational potential and commercial challenges of Arctic shipping. The 2,758 TEU vessel arrived at Busan Port...
articles.body: South Korea has completed its first container shipping round trip between Asia and Europe via the Northern Sea Route, with the PanStar Acro returning to Busan after a 50-day voyage that highlighted both the operational potential and commercial challenges of Arctic shipping. The 2,758 TEU vessel arrived at Busan Port on 11 October, having departed on 22 August as part of a government-backed trial designed to assess the feasibility of container transport through Arctic waters. Although the voyage was completed successfully, the ship returned carrying only empty containers, raising questions about cargo availability and the commercial viability of regular services along the route. PanStar Acro completes 50-day round trip Operated by PanStar, the vessel departed Busan New Port on 22 August and entered Arctic waters on 31 August before continuing through the Northern Sea Route towards Europe. It reached Felixstowe in the United Kingdom on 12 September, followed by Rotterdam in the Netherlands and Gdansk in Poland, before beginning its return journey to South Korea. The vessel completed the round trip in 50 days, compared with an initial target of approximately 45 days outlined by the South Korean Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries. The trial forms part of South Korea’s efforts to evaluate the Northern Sea Route as an alternative maritime corridor connecting Northeast Asia and Northern Europe. According to the ministry’s initial estimates, the Arctic passage could reduce sailing distances between Busan and Rotterdam by approximately 35% compared with the conventional route through the Suez Canal.
